t110g3x6.t: Treaty establishing a Constitution for Europe

teile.einleitung: The Treaty establishing a Constitution for Europe was meant to put the EU on a new footing. It was signed in Rome in 2004. In 2005, however, it failed in referendums in France and the Netherlands.
wichtigste: The draft was drawn up by the European Convention under Valéry Giscard d'Estaing.
The treaty was signed in Rome on 29 October 2004.
In February 2005 Spain was the first country to approve it in a referendum.
France and the Netherlands said no in 2005.
After that the EU took a period of reflection.
A “Union Minister for Foreign Affairs” was planned.
Much of its content later went into the Treaty of Lisbon.

abschnitte.text: The draft was worked out by the **European Convention**. It met from **2002 to 2003** and was made up of representatives of governments, parliaments and EU bodies. It was **chaired** by the former French president **Valéry Giscard d'Estaing**. The treaty was meant to combine the existing treaties into a single text. On **29 October 2004** the heads of state and government signed it in **Rome**, in the same place as the founding treaties of 1957.

The treaty named the **flag**, **anthem**, **motto**, currency and **Europe Day** as symbols of the Union. For the top foreign affairs representative the title **“Union Minister for Foreign Affairs”** was planned. Critics felt that such state-like terms made the EU look like a **superstate**.

In **Spain**, on **20 February 2005** around three quarters of voters said **yes**, with a low turnout of about 42 per cent. But then **France** voted **no** on **29 May 2005** with around 55 per cent. On **1 June 2005** the **Netherlands** followed with around 62 per cent no. **Luxembourg** nevertheless approved the treaty on **10 July 2005** with around 57 per cent. Other countries postponed their planned votes.

In **June 2005** the European Council decided on a **period of reflection**, a time for thinking things over. Only in **2007** was agreement reached on a new reform project **without the word constitution**. This became the **Treaty of Lisbon**. Symbols such as the flag and anthem were left out of the new treaty text but are still used in everyday life. The title “Foreign Minister” was also dropped, but the tasks largely remained under a different name.

gewusst: France and the Netherlands, which said no, were both among the six founding states of European integration.
The European anthem is the melody of the “Ode to Joy” from Beethoven's Ninth Symphony.

teile.einleitung: The European Union was founded with the Treaty of Maastricht. It was signed in 1992 in the Dutch city of Maastricht. It also prepared the way for the euro and introduced citizenship of the Union.
wichtigste: The treaty was signed on 7 February 1992.
It came into force on 1 November 1993.
It created the European Union.
It set out the path to economic and monetary union and the euro.
It introduced citizenship of the Union.
Afterwards the EU rested on three pillars.
Denmark said no in a first referendum.

abschnitte.text: **Maastricht** lies in the south of the **Netherlands**, near the borders with Belgium and Germany. The **Treaty on European Union** was signed there on **7 February 1992**. After ratification in all member states it came into force on **1 November 1993**. It is regarded as the **founding treaty** of the EU.

The structure of the EU is often described with a **three-pillar model**. The **first pillar** was the **European Communities**. The **second pillar** was the **Common Foreign and Security Policy** (CFSP). The **third pillar** was cooperation in **justice and home affairs**. The second and third pillars were organised on an **intergovernmental** basis, so the governments kept more power there.

The treaty set out the path to **economic and monetary union**. This gave rise to the **euro**, which has also been used as cash since 2002. Any country that wants to introduce the euro must meet the **Maastricht criteria**. One of them: the annual **government deficit** may be no more than **3 per cent** of gross domestic product. Gross domestic product is the value of all the goods and services of a country in one year.

Maastricht brought **citizenship of the Union**. Every person who holds the nationality of an EU country is at the same time a **citizen of the Union**. This means, for example, that you may move freely in other EU countries and vote in local elections where you live. Citizenship of the Union adds to your own nationality but does not replace it.

In **Denmark** voters narrowly said **no** in the first vote in **1992**. After **special arrangements** for Denmark they approved it in a second vote. In **Switzerland**, too, there was a vote on Europe at that time: on **6 December 1992** the people and the cantons rejected joining the **European Economic Area**.

gewusst: Euro coins and banknotes only arrived in people's purses and wallets around ten years after Maastricht was signed.
Denmark still has an exemption today and has not introduced the euro.

teile.einleitung: The United Nations, UN for short, is the largest organisation of states in the world. Its most important aim is to secure peace all over the world and to encourage cooperation between countries. Almost all the states on Earth are members, including Switzerland.
wichtigste: The UN aims to secure peace all over the world.
It was founded in 1945 after the Second World War.
Today 193 states are members of the UN.
The name “United Nations” means that countries have joined together in order to act together.
Its headquarters are in New York; Geneva is an important location.
The UN has six official languages: Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish.
Switzerland has been a member since 2002.

abschnitte.text: The Second World War cost many millions of people their lives. Afterwards the states wanted to prevent anything like it from ever happening again. On 26 June 1945, 50 states signed the **UN Charter** in San Francisco; Poland joined as the 51st founding member. It came into force on 24 October 1945, which is why this day is United Nations Day. The name had been suggested by the American president Franklin D. Roosevelt.

The UN wants to secure **world peace** and settle conflicts peacefully. It works for human rights, which were set down in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948. It also helps with hunger, diseases and natural disasters. Since 2015 it has been pursuing the **2030 Agenda** with 17 goals for sustainable development, for example zero hunger and quality education.

The UN has six main bodies. All states are represented in the **General Assembly**, and the **Security Council** is responsible for peace and security. In addition there are the Economic and Social Council, the International Court of Justice in The Hague, the Secretariat and the Trusteeship Council, which is inactive today. The Secretariat is led by the Secretary-General; since 2017 this has been António Guterres from Portugal, whose term ends at the end of 2026.

The UN includes many specialised agencies and programmes. Examples are the World Health Organization (WHO), the children's agency UNICEF, the refugee agency UNHCR and UNESCO. In conflicts the UN sends peacekeeping troops, who are called **Blue Helmets** because of their light blue helmets. The UN flag shows a map of the world surrounded by olive branches as a sign of peace.

For a long time Switzerland stayed outside the UN because of its neutrality. In 1986 the people still clearly rejected joining. On 3 March 2002 they narrowly agreed, and in September 2002 Switzerland became a member. Apart from New York, **Geneva** is the most important UN location, with the Palais des Nations and many organisations. From 2023 to 2024 Switzerland even sat on the Security Council.

begriffe.erklaerung: A founding treaty that sets out the aims and rules of an organisation.
The highest official of the UN, who leads its administration.
A country that has joined an organisation.
A UN plan with 17 goals for a better world by the year 2030.

gewusst: Switzerland was the first country to join the UN through a popular vote.
In front of the Palais des Nations in Geneva stands the “Broken Chair”, a huge chair with a broken leg that remembers the victims of landmines.
In 2001 the UN and its Secretary-General at the time, Kofi Annan, were jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

teile.einleitung: On 17 February 2008 Kosovo declared its independence from Serbia. Since then Kosovo, in its own view, has been an independent state. Many countries have recognised it, but Serbia and some other states have not.
wichtigste: Kosovo declared its independence on 17 February 2008.
The capital is Pristina.
Over 90 per cent of the population are Kosovo Albanians.
Serbia does not recognise its independence (as of 2026).
In 2010 the International Court of Justice found no breach of international law.
The Swiss Army has been in Kosovo with Swisscoy since 1999.
In Kosovo people pay with the euro.

abschnitte.text: **Kosovo** lies in the Balkans in south-eastern Europe. The **capital** is **Pristina**, where the parliament and government are based. Over **90 per cent** of the people are **Kosovo Albanians**. **Serbs** live mainly in the north. The **euro** is used as the currency, although Kosovo is not part of the eurozone. Before that, people used the Deutschmark.

For a long time Kosovo belonged to **Serbia** and therefore to Yugoslavia. In the 1990s tensions grew between the Albanian majority and the Serbian government. In **1998 and 1999** the **Kosovo War** took place. From **March to June 1999** **NATO** attacked targets in Serbia with air strikes. After that the Serbian troops withdrew and the **UN** took over the administration of Kosovo.

On **17 February 2008** the parliament in **Pristina** proclaimed **independence**. Many people celebrated in the streets. Many states soon recognised Kosovo, including **Switzerland**. However, **Serbia** still regards Kosovo as its own province (as of 2026). Some other states such as **Spain** or **Russia** do not recognise Kosovo either.

Serbia wanted the question settled legally. Through the **UN General Assembly** it asked for an **advisory opinion** from the **International Court of Justice** in The Hague. In **2010** the court concluded that the declaration of independence itself **did not violate international law**. But whether Kosovo is a state is decided by the other states through their recognition.

**Swisscoy** has been deployed in Kosovo since **1999**. It is a contingent of the **Swiss Army** in the international peacekeeping force **KFOR**. It is the Swiss Army's largest **mission abroad**. Switzerland and Kosovo are also linked by many people: a large community with roots in Kosovo lives in Switzerland.

gewusst: Swisscoy is made up of “Swiss” and “company”, the English word for a military company.
Kosovo is one of the youngest states in Europe.

teile.einleitung: Vatican City is the smallest country in the world. It lies in the middle of Rome and is the seat of the Pope. The Pope is protected by the Swiss Guard.
wichtigste: Vatican City is smaller than half a square kilometre.
The head of state is the Pope, the head of the Catholic Church.
Fewer than 1000 people live here.
The Swiss Guard has protected the Pope since 1506.
The great church is called St Peter's Basilica.
The flag is yellow and white.
Leo XIV has been Pope since May 2025.

abschnitte.text: **Vatican City** lies in the middle of **Rome**, the capital of Italy. It is smaller than **half a square kilometre**. No other country is so small. A wall surrounds large parts of its territory. Vatican City has existed as a separate state since the **Lateran Treaty** of **1929** with Italy.

The head of state is the **Pope**. He is the head of the **Catholic Church** and holds all state power in Vatican City. He is elected by the **cardinals** in the **Sistine Chapel**. In **May 2025** they elected **Robert Prevost**. He took the name **Leo XIV** and is the first Pope from the **USA**.

The **Swiss Guard** protects the Pope. The first Swiss guards came to Rome in **1506**. It is considered the oldest army in the world that still exists. The guards are Catholic **Swiss men** and wear colourful uniforms in **blue, yellow and red**. Every year on **6 May** new guards are sworn in. This day recalls 1527, when many guards lost their lives defending the Pope.

**St Peter's Basilica** is one of the largest churches in the world. The Pope celebrates large **services** there. In front of the church lies the wide **St Peter's Square**, where tens of thousands of people often gather. The **Vatican Museums** with their precious art treasures are also famous. The ceiling of the Sistine Chapel was painted by **Michelangelo**.

Only **a few hundred people** live in Vatican City, fewer than 1000. Many of them are clergy or **Swiss Guards**. No country has fewer inhabitants. The **flag** is **yellow** on the left and **white** on the right. The white part shows two crossed **keys** and the **papal crown**.

gewusst: Vatican City has its own railway station and its own post office, and it issues its own stamps.
Anyone who wants to join the Swiss Guard must have completed recruit school in the Swiss Army.

teile.einleitung: Ursula von der Leyen is a German politician. Since December 2019 she has been President of the European Commission, the first woman in this office. Before that she was a federal minister in Germany several times.
wichtigste: Ursula von der Leyen has led the EU Commission since 1 December 2019.
She is German and a member of the CDU.
She was born in Brussels in 1958.
From 2013 to 2019 she was Germany's defence minister.
In July 2024 she was elected for a second term.
In 2019 her Commission presented the European Green Deal.

abschnitte.text: Ursula von der Leyen was born in **Brussels** in **1958**. Her father worked there for the European institutions. Later the family moved to Lower Saxony in Germany. Von der Leyen studied **medicine** and worked as a doctor. She is a member of the **CDU**, the Christian Democratic Union. In the European Parliament the CDU belongs to the **European People's Party**.

In Germany she was first a minister in the federal state of **Lower Saxony**. From **2005** she was part of **Angela Merkel's** federal government. She was **Minister for Family Affairs** and then **Minister of Labour**. From **2013 to 2019** she was **Federal Minister of Defence**, the first woman in this office. After that she moved to Brussels.

The **European Commission** proposes laws and makes sure that EU law is respected. The President is proposed by the **European Council**. After that the **European Parliament** must approve with a majority of its members. Ursula von der Leyen has been in office since **1 December 2019**. In **July 2024** Parliament confirmed her for a further **five years**.

In **December 2019** her Commission presented the **European Green Deal**. With it the EU is to become **climate neutral** by **2050**. Her time in office was also shaped by the coronavirus pandemic and the war in Ukraine. The Commission has **27 members**, because each member state provides one, the President included. In December 2024, together with the Federal Council in **Bern**, she announced the conclusion of negotiations on new agreements between Switzerland and the EU.

gewusst: As well as German, Ursula von der Leyen also speaks fluent French and English.
She was the first woman to head the German Ministry of Defence and also the first to head the EU Commission.

teile.einleitung: Crimes against humanity are extremely serious acts committed as part of a large attack on the civilian population. They are among the worst crimes known to international law. The International Criminal Court and Swiss courts can prosecute them.
wichtigste: The act must be part of a widespread or systematic attack on civilians.
Today they are set out in Article 7 of the Rome Statute.
They can also be committed in peacetime.
The term was first used in 1915 in connection with the massacres of the Armenians.
Unlike genocide, no intent to destroy a group is needed.
Apartheid and enforced disappearance also count.
In Switzerland these crimes never become time-barred.

abschnitte.text: In **1915** **France**, **Britain** and **Russia** warned the Ottoman government about the **massacres of the Armenians**. They spoke of crimes “against humanity” and announced that they would hold those responsible personally to account. The term later found its way into **international law**. After the Second World War it was applied in the **Nuremberg trials**. At that time these crimes only counted in connection with a **war**.

An important pioneer was the international lawyer **Hersch Lauterpacht**. He advised the British prosecution at Nuremberg. Lauterpacht put the protection of the **individual person** at the centre. His approach differed from that of the lawyer **Raphael Lemkin**, who coined the term **genocide** and stressed the protection of **groups**.

Today these crimes are set out in **Article 7** of the **Rome Statute** of the International Criminal Court. An act such as murder, enslavement, deportation or torture becomes a crime against humanity if it is part of a **widespread or systematic attack** against a **civilian population**. The perpetrator must know this. A link with a war is **no longer needed**; the acts can also happen in **peacetime**.

The Statute expressly mentions **apartheid**. This means a regime in which one group systematically oppresses another. The term comes from **South Africa**. **Enforced disappearance** also counts: the state arrests people and keeps their fate or whereabouts secret. This method became known, for example, in **military dictatorships in Latin America**. These crimes differ from genocide in that no intent to **destroy** a protected group is needed.

Switzerland also punishes crimes against humanity in its **Criminal Code** (SCC). Under **Article 101 SCC**, genocide, crimes against humanity and serious war crimes are **not subject to any time limit**. This means they can still be prosecuted even after a very long time. In Switzerland the **Office of the Attorney General** is responsible for such cases.

gewusst: Hersch Lauterpacht and Raphael Lemkin had both studied at the university in Lemberg, today's Lviv.
Crimes against humanity can also be committed by groups that are not a government.

teile.einleitung: The Treaty of Amsterdam is a reform treaty of the European Union. It was signed in 1997 and came into force in 1999. It strengthened the European Parliament and made Schengen part of EU law.
wichtigste: The treaty was signed on 2 October 1997.
It came into force on 1 May 1999.
The Schengen acquis was taken over into EU law.
Javier Solana became the first High Representative for foreign policy.
The European Parliament was strengthened through more co-decision.
A chapter on employment and enhanced cooperation were added.
An area of freedom, security and justice became a goal.

abschnitte.text: The **Treaty of Amsterdam** amended the existing EU treaties, above all the **Treaty of Maastricht**. It was signed on **2 October 1997** and came into force on **1 May 1999**. The aim was to make the EU more democratic and better able to act. In addition, the articles of the treaties were renumbered.

The **Schengen Agreements** on open internal borders had come about outside the EU treaties. Amsterdam took this **Schengen acquis** over into **EU law**. Areas such as **asylum**, **immigration** and **visas** were moved to the Community level. As an overarching goal the treaty named an **area of freedom, security and justice**. Switzerland has applied Schengen since 2008 as an associated country without being an EU member.

The treaty extended the **co-decision procedure** to many areas and simplified it. This put the **European Parliament** on an equal footing with the **Council** on many legislative questions. Amsterdam also created the office of **High Representative** for the Common Foreign and Security Policy. The first holder of the office, from **1999 to 2009**, was the Spaniard **Javier Solana**, previously Secretary General of NATO.

Because of high **unemployment**, a new **chapter on employment** was added to the EC Treaty. The member states committed themselves to coordinating their employment policies. This gave rise to the **European Employment Strategy**. **Enhanced cooperation** was also new: a group of states may go ahead in one area without all of them taking part. Later it was used, for example, for the **EU patent**.

Amsterdam also created a procedure that today is found in **Article 7** of the EU Treaty. If a member state seriously and persistently breaches the **basic values** such as democracy or the rule of law, certain rights can be taken away from it. These include its **voting rights in the Council**. **Expulsion** from the EU, on the other hand, is not provided for.

gewusst: Because Amsterdam renumbered many articles, some provisions have had a completely different number ever since.
Javier Solana was the face of EU foreign policy for around ten years.

teile.einleitung: The Treaty of Lisbon is the treaty that shapes the European Union today. It was signed in Lisbon in 2007 and has applied since 2009. It gave the EU new offices, more citizens' rights and, for the first time, a rule for leaving.
wichtigste: The treaty was signed in Lisbon in December 2007.
It came into force on 1 December 2009.
It replaced the failed EU constitution.
Since then Article 50 has governed a country's withdrawal.
The Charter of Fundamental Rights became legally binding.
The permanent President of the European Council and the High Representative are new.
A European Citizens' Initiative needs one million signatures.

abschnitte.text: In **2005** **France** and the **Netherlands** rejected the planned **EU constitution** in referendums. Much of its content was then taken over into a new treaty. This was signed in **December 2007** in **Lisbon**, the capital of **Portugal**. Portugal held the Council presidency at the time. After all the countries had approved it, the treaty came into force on **1 December 2009**.

The treaty created the office of a **permanent President of the European Council**. The first holder of the office, from **2009 to 2014**, was the Belgian **Herman Van Rompuy**. Before that the presidency changed every six months. The **High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy** is also new. This person leads the EU's foreign policy and is at the same time **Vice-President of the Commission**. The role is often called the EU's foreign policy chief.

The **Charter of Fundamental Rights** has existed since 2000. Since the Treaty of Lisbon it has been just as **binding** as the EU treaties. In addition, the EU as a whole gained its own **legal personality**. It can therefore conclude international agreements itself. The **European Citizens' Initiative** is also new: with **one million signatures** from at least **seven** countries, citizens can ask the Commission to propose a law.

Since 2014 the **double majority** has applied for a **qualified majority** in the Council. A decision needs at least **55 per cent** of the member states, together representing at least **65 per cent** of the EU population. For the first time the treaty also governs a country's **withdrawal**, namely in **Article 50** of the EU Treaty. The **United Kingdom** used this article for **Brexit**.

gewusst: Before the Treaty of Lisbon there was no rule at all in the EU treaties on how a country could leave.
The United Kingdom was the first country to leave the EU using Article 50.

teile.einleitung: The UN Security Council is the most powerful body of the United Nations. It is responsible for keeping peace and security in the world. Unlike the General Assembly, it can make decisions that all states must follow.
wichtigste: The Security Council has 15 members: 5 permanent and 10 non-permanent.
The five permanent members are the USA, Russia, China, France and the United Kingdom.
Each permanent member has a right of veto and can block a resolution on its own.
The non-permanent members are elected for two years by the General Assembly.
The Security Council can decide on sanctions and send peace missions.
Switzerland was a member for the first time in 2023 and 2024.
Reform is often discussed because the membership no longer reflects today's world.

abschnitte.text: According to the UN Charter, the **Security Council** has the main responsibility for world peace. It meets when there are wars or dangerous conflicts and can call on the opposing sides to make peace. It can decide on **sanctions**, for example an arms embargo or freezing money. In the most extreme case it may even allow military force. It also sends peacekeeping troops, the so-called Blue Helmets, to crisis areas.

The five permanent members are the USA, Russia, China, France and the United Kingdom, the most important victorious powers of the Second World War. In 1991 Russia took over the seat of the Soviet Union. Until 1971 China's seat was held by the Republic of China on Taiwan, then it passed to the People's Republic of China. In addition there are ten **non-permanent members**, each elected for two years. The Council has had 15 seats since 1965; before that there were 11.

A decision needs at least nine votes in favour. But each permanent member can block a resolution on its own with its **veto**. This often means the Council cannot act in major conflicts, for example when a permanent member is itself involved. Since 2022 the General Assembly meets after every veto to debate it.

Many states think the Council shows the world of 1945 and not the world of today. Africa and Latin America, for example, have no permanent seat. India, Brazil, Germany and Japan would like a permanent seat and work together for this as the **G4**. But **reform** is difficult because the Charter would have to be changed and the permanent members would have to agree.

In 2022 Switzerland was elected to the Council by a large majority for the years 2023 and 2024. It held the **presidency**, which changes every month, in May 2023 and October 2024. Among other things, Switzerland worked for the protection of civilians and for climate security. Before it stood as a candidate, there was debate about whether a seat was compatible with neutrality.

begriffe.erklaerung: Latin for “I forbid”. A single no that prevents a decision.
A penalty, for example a trade ban, to put pressure on a country.
Soldiers of the UN peacekeeping forces, named after their light blue helmets.
A country that always sits on the Council and never has to be re-elected.

gewusst: Over the course of history, the Soviet Union and Russia have used the veto most often.
On the Security Council the presidency changes every month, in turn according to the English alphabetical order of the countries' names.

teile.einleitung: The UNHCR is the UN Refugee Agency. It protects people who have had to flee their homes because of war, violence or persecution. Its headquarters are in Geneva, and it has already received the Nobel Peace Prize twice.
wichtigste: The main task of the UNHCR is to protect and support refugees worldwide.
UNHCR stands for “United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees”.
The UNHCR was founded in 1950 and is based in Geneva.
Its work is based on the Geneva Refugee Convention of 1951.
The agency received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1954 and 1981.
In 2025 well over 100 million people worldwide had been forced to flee.
The UNHCR provides refugees with tents, water and food and helps them build a new life.

abschnitte.text: The **UNHCR** was created by the UN General Assembly on 14 December 1950 and began work in 1951. Originally it was only meant to help refugees from the Second World War in Europe for a few years. But because new crises kept arising, it became a permanent organisation. Today it works in over 130 countries. It is led by the UN **High Commissioner for Refugees**.

The **Geneva Refugee Convention** of 1951 sets out who counts as a refugee. A refugee is a person who is persecuted because of their origin, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership of a group. The most important principle is called **non-refoulement**: nobody may be sent back to a country where they face persecution. The UNHCR makes sure that states keep to these rules.

When many people flee at once, the UNHCR sets up **refugee camps**. It hands out tents, blankets, drinking water and hygiene items and provides medical help. It also helps children in the camps to go to school. However, many refugees do not live in camps but in towns and cities in neighbouring countries.

The UNHCR looks for three possible solutions for refugees. The first is voluntary return when it is safe at home again. The second is integration in the host country. The third is **resettlement** in another country that takes in especially vulnerable people, as Switzerland also does.

The UNHCR's headquarters are in Geneva, very close to other UN buildings. Switzerland is an important donor and works closely with the agency. In Switzerland the State Secretariat for Migration examines whether someone receives asylum. Another well-known figure is **Sadruddin Aga Khan**, who was High Commissioner for Refugees from 1965 to 1977 and lived for a long time on Lake Geneva.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who has had to leave their home because they are persecuted or threatened there.
Protection that a state grants to a persecuted person.
The ban on sending someone back to a country where they face danger.
People who have had to flee within their own country.

gewusst: About 40 per cent of all people who have been forced to flee are children.
Every year the UNHCR awards the Nansen Refugee Award, named after the Norwegian polar explorer Fridtjof Nansen, who already helped refugees for the League of Nations.

teile.einleitung: The USMCA is a free trade agreement between the USA, Mexico and Canada. It has been in force since 2020 and replaced the older NAFTA agreement. Together the three countries form a large economic area in North America.
wichtigste: The USMCA includes the USA, Mexico and Canada.
It came into force on 1 July 2020.
It replaced the NAFTA agreement, which had applied since 1994.
In Mexico it is called T-MEC, in Canada CUSMA.
Strict rules apply to cars: around 75 per cent of their value must come from the region.
The three states review the agreement every six years.

abschnitte.text: A **free trade agreement** lowers or removes **customs duties** on goods between the partner countries. A customs duty is a fee that has to be paid when goods cross a border. Without customs duties, goods from the partner country become cheaper. A **common currency** or open borders for people are not part of a free trade agreement. Switzerland also has many free trade agreements, for example with the EU.

The **North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA)** came into force on **1 January 1994**. At the time it created one of the largest free trade areas in the world. In **2017** the three countries began to negotiate a new agreement. The **USMCA** came into force on **1 July 2020** and replaced NAFTA. The name stands for “United States, Mexico, Canada Agreement”.

Each country calls the agreement something slightly different. In the USA it is called the **USMCA**. In **Mexico** people say **T-MEC**, short for “Tratado entre México, Estados Unidos y Canadá”. In **Canada** it is called **CUSMA**. In all three names the country's own name comes first.

The **rules of origin** for the **car industry** are especially important. For a car to be traded free of customs duties, around **75 per cent** of its value must come from North America. This is meant to secure jobs in the region. The agreement also contains rules on **workers' rights** and on trade over the internet. Every **six years** the three states must **review** the agreement together; the first review was scheduled for July 2026.

gewusst: Goods worth billions of dollars are traded between the three USMCA countries every day.
Many car parts cross borders in North America several times on their way to becoming a finished car.

teile.einleitung: UNAIDS is the joint United Nations programme against HIV and AIDS. It coordinates the work of several UN organisations in this field. Its headquarters are in Geneva.
wichtigste: UNAIDS fights HIV and AIDS worldwide.
It was decided on in 1994 and has been working since 1996.
Its headquarters are in Geneva, close to the WHO.
Several UN organisations such as the WHO, UNICEF and UNDP work together in it.
World AIDS Day is on 1 December every year.
The red ribbon shows solidarity with people living with HIV.
UNAIDS wants to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030.

abschnitte.text: **HIV** stands for “human immunodeficiency virus”, a virus that weakens the **immune system**. It attacks the body's defences, the so-called **immune system**. Without treatment, the disease **AIDS** can develop from it after some years. The body can then hardly defend itself against many illnesses. Today there are **medicines** that allow people with HIV to live long and well. So far, however, HIV cannot be cured.

UNAIDS was decided on in **1994** and began its work in **1996**. It took over tasks from an older programme of the **World Health Organization (WHO)**. What is special is that UNAIDS links several UN organisations. These **cosponsors** include, for example, the **WHO**, the children's fund **UNICEF** and the development programme **UNDP**. Together they are meant to tackle HIV more effectively.

UNAIDS has its headquarters in **Geneva**. The WHO, with which UNAIDS works closely, is also there. Geneva is an important place for global health policy. From here UNAIDS collects figures, advises governments and supports programmes in many countries. Countries in southern Africa are especially affected.

Since **1988**, **World AIDS Day** has been held on **1 December** every year. It remembers the people who have died of AIDS and calls for **solidarity**. Its well-known symbol is the **red ribbon**. It became known in **1991**. Anyone who wears it shows that people with HIV should not be excluded.

UNAIDS has set itself clear targets. The first “95” means that **95 per cent** of people with HIV know about their infection. The other targets concern **treatment** and a strongly suppressed **viral load**, meaning very few viruses in the body. The big goal is to end AIDS as a public health threat **by 2030**. It is part of the UN's **2030 Agenda**.

gewusst: People who are treated effectively often have so few viruses in their blood that they can no longer be measured with ordinary tests.
In Switzerland, the Swiss AIDS Federation (Aids-Hilfe Schweiz) has supported people with HIV since 1985.

teile.einleitung: UNRWA is the United Nations agency for Palestine refugees in the Near East. It runs schools and health centres and provides social help. Two Swiss men led the agency for a long time.
wichtigste: UNRWA helps Palestine refugees and their descendants.
The UN General Assembly founded it in December 1949.
It is active in five areas in the Middle East.
It runs hundreds of schools for refugee children.
Its money comes mainly from voluntary contributions by states.
Philippe Lazzarini from Switzerland led it from 2020 to 2026.

abschnitte.text: After the first war between Israel and Arab states in 1948, many Palestinians lost their homes. The **UN General Assembly** therefore founded **UNRWA** in **December 1949**. It began its work in **May 1950**. It cares for **Palestine refugees** and their descendants. Its mandate is **limited in time** and is **extended** by the General Assembly by a few years at a time.

UNRWA works in **five fields of operation**: in **Jordan**, in **Lebanon**, in **Syria**, in the **West Bank** including East Jerusalem and in the **Gaza Strip**. Its **headquarters** are in **Amman** in Jordan and in **Gaza**. Unlike the UN Refugee Agency **UNHCR**, which looks after refugees all over the world, UNRWA is responsible only for Palestine refugees.

UNRWA runs **hundreds of schools** for refugee children. There are also **health centres** and **social help** for poor families. In crises it also hands out food and other emergency aid. Many staff members come from the region themselves. Only a small part of the money comes from the regular UN budget; most of it comes from **voluntary contributions** by states and organisations. Switzerland also supports the agency.

UNRWA is led by a **Commissioner-General**. From **2014 to 2019** this was the Swiss **Pierre Krähenbühl**, previously director of operations at the **ICRC**. From **March 2020 to the end of March 2026** **Philippe Lazzarini** from Neuchâtel led the agency. He too had previously worked for a long time for the ICRC and the UN. UNRWA's work is judged differently in politics, and there are repeated disputes about its funding.

gewusst: UNRWA is the abbreviation of the English name “United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East”.
Measured by the number of staff, UNRWA is one of the largest organisations of the UN.

teile.einleitung: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations, ASEAN for short, is a union of states in Southeast Asia. It was founded in 1967 and aims to promote peace, cooperation and the economy in the region. Since 2025 it has had eleven members.
wichtigste: ASEAN was founded on 8 August 1967 with the Bangkok Declaration.
The founding members were Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand.
The secretariat is in Jakarta.
East Timor has been the eleventh member since October 2025.
The “ASEAN Way” is based on consensus and non-interference.
Since its Charter of 2008, ASEAN has had its own legal personality.
The RCEP free trade agreement has applied since 2022.

abschnitte.text: On **8 August 1967** the foreign ministers of five states signed the **Bangkok Declaration**. The founding members were **Indonesia**, **Malaysia**, the **Philippines**, **Singapore** and **Thailand**. Later other countries joined, for example **Vietnam** in **1995** and **Cambodia** in 1999. In **October 2025** **East Timor** became the **eleventh member** at the summit in Kuala Lumpur. The **secretariat** was set up in 1976 and is based in **Jakarta**.

The declaration of 1967 was not yet a legally binding treaty. Only the **ASEAN Charter**, which came into force in **December 2008**, turned the association into an intergovernmental organisation with **legal personality**. This means that ASEAN can now conclude treaties itself. Unlike the EU, however, it cannot make laws for its members.

The **“ASEAN Way”** is typical of ASEAN. Traditionally the states decide by **consensus**, meaning unanimously. They also do not interfere in each other's **internal affairs**. Supporters see this as a way of avoiding disputes. Critics see it as a weakness, for example in dealing with **Myanmar**. After the military coup there, ASEAN agreed a **Five-Point Consensus** in **April 2021**, but the military government hardly put it into practice.

The ASEAN states want to make trade between them easier. In addition there is the **RCEP** free trade agreement (Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership). It was signed by 15 states in **2020** and came into force on **1 January 2022**. As well as the ASEAN states, it includes **China**, **Japan**, **South Korea**, **Australia** and **New Zealand**. Through **EFTA**, Switzerland has free trade agreements with several ASEAN states, for example with Singapore and Indonesia.

gewusst: Measured by population and economic output, the RCEP is considered the largest free trade area in the world.
Swiss voters voted on the agreement with Indonesia in 2021 and narrowly approved it.

teile.einleitung: The principle of distinction is a basic rule of international humanitarian law, the law that applies in war. It requires the parties to a war always to distinguish between soldiers and civilians. Attacks may only be directed against military targets.
wichtigste: Art. 48 of Additional Protocol I contains the basic rule of distinction.
Attacks may only be directed against military targets.
In case of doubt, a person counts as a civilian.
Indiscriminate attacks are forbidden.
Civilian harm must not be excessive in relation to the military advantage.
In 1996 the ICJ called the principle of distinction a cardinal principle.
Using civilians as shields is forbidden.

abschnitte.text: The idea is old. The **St Petersburg Declaration** of **1868** stated that the only legitimate aim in war is **to weaken the enemy's military forces**. It also banned small explosive projectiles under 400 grams. Later the principle was developed in the **Geneva Conventions** of 1949 and their **Additional Protocols** of 1977. Switzerland is the depositary of these treaties, and the **ICRC** in Geneva works to make sure they are respected.

**Art. 48** of Additional Protocol I (AP I) requires a distinction to be made **at all times** between the **civilian population** and **combatants**. In the same way, civilian objects must be distinguished from **military targets**. According to **Art. 43**, **combatants** are the members of the armed forces of a party to the conflict, except medical and religious personnel. They may take part in fighting and become **prisoners of war** if captured. In 1996 the **International Court of Justice** called the principle a **cardinal principle** of international humanitarian law.

If it is unclear whether someone is a civilian, then under **Art. 50** the person counts as a **civilian** in case of doubt. A building that is normally used for civilian purposes is also not considered a military target in case of doubt. Under **Art. 51(3)** a civilian loses their protection only **for as long as** they take a direct part in hostilities. After that they are protected again.

**Indiscriminate attacks** are forbidden. These are attacks that are not directed at a specific military target or that use weapons which cannot be aimed precisely. Area bombing of whole cities also falls under this. According to the **principle of proportionality**, an attack is also forbidden if the expected civilian harm is **excessive** in relation to the concrete military advantage.

Under **Art. 51(7)** parties to a conflict may not use the presence of civilians to shield military targets from attack. This is called using **human shields**. If one side breaks this rule, the other side is still bound by its **obligations** towards the civilians. This shows that the protection of the civilian population always applies, even if the enemy does not keep to the rules.

gewusst: The Geneva Conventions of 1949 have been ratified by every state in the world.
According to the ICJ's 1996 advisory opinion, weapons that cannot distinguish at all between soldiers and civilians are forbidden.

teile.einleitung: UNESCO World Heritage includes especially valuable places of humanity and nature. These include old cities, buildings and unique landscapes. Switzerland also has several World Heritage Sites.
wichtigste: UNESCO keeps a list of cultural and natural heritage from all over the world.
The Old City of Bern and the Abbey of St Gall have been World Heritage since 1983.
Jungfrau-Aletsch has been a natural World Heritage Site since 2001.
The Albula and Bernina lines of the Rhaetian Railway have been World Heritage since 2008.
The castles of Bellinzona and Lavaux are also on the list.
Famous examples worldwide are the Pyramids of Giza and the Great Wall of China.

abschnitte.text: **UNESCO** is the UN organisation for education, science and culture. In **1972** the states agreed on a convention to protect the world's **cultural and natural heritage**. Places of outstanding value can be put on the **World Heritage List**. A committee decides on new entries every year. The countries commit themselves to protecting and caring for their World Heritage Sites.

The **Old City of Bern** with its arcades and fountains has been World Heritage since **1983**. In the same year the **Abbey of St Gall** with its famous **Abbey Library** was added. Since **2000** the three **castles of Bellinzona** in Ticino with the town wall have been on the list. The **Lavaux vineyard terraces** on Lake Geneva between Lausanne and Montreux have been World Heritage since **2007**.

The **Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch** area became a natural World Heritage Site in **2001**. It contains the **Aletsch Glacier**, the largest glacier in the Alps. Since **2008** the **Albula and Bernina lines** of the **Rhaetian Railway** in the Grisons have also been World Heritage. The trains run over many **viaducts** and through **spiral tunnels**, in which the line winds upwards in a circle.

There are more than a thousand World Heritage Sites worldwide. The **Pyramids of Giza** in Egypt are over 4000 years old and have been World Heritage since **1979**. The **Great Wall of China** is thousands of kilometres long and has been on the list since **1987**. The **Great Barrier Reef** off Australia is the largest coral reef on Earth and has been a natural World Heritage Site since **1981**.

gewusst: A World Heritage Site can be put on the List of World Heritage in Danger if it is under threat, for example from war or building projects.
The Benedictine Convent of St John at Müstair in the Grisons has also been World Heritage since 1983.

teile.einleitung: UNICEF is the United Nations children's agency. It works for the rights and well-being of children all over the world, so that they grow up healthy, go to school and are protected from violence. UNICEF helps in crises and disasters, but also every day in poor countries.
wichtigste: UNICEF works for the rights and well-being of children worldwide.
The children's agency was founded on 11 December 1946.
Its headquarters are in New York.
UNICEF is active in over 190 countries and territories.
Its work is paid for only by voluntary donations from states, companies and private individuals.
In 1965 UNICEF received the Nobel Peace Prize.
Its work is based on the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child of 1989.

abschnitte.text: The name **UNICEF** comes from the original English name “United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund”. The agency was founded after the Second World War to help starving children in Europe. Later it extended its work to children in Africa, Asia and Latin America. UNICEF has been a permanent body of the UN since 1953.

Every year UNICEF buys huge quantities of **vaccines** and brings them even to remote villages. In this way children are protected against diseases such as measles and polio. For severely malnourished children, UNICEF hands out a nourishing peanut paste that can be eaten without cooking. The agency also builds wells and toilets so that children have clean water.

UNICEF helps to build schools, hand out school materials and train teachers. In war zones it sets up emergency schools and safe play areas for children. It campaigns against **child labour**, child marriage and the use of child soldiers. It is especially important that girls are also allowed to learn.

On 20 November 1989 the UN adopted the **Convention on the Rights of the Child**. It includes, for example, the right to education, to health, to play and leisure and to protection from violence. Almost all the states of the world have recognised this convention, Switzerland in 1997. UNICEF makes sure that children's rights are put into practice.

The committee **UNICEF Switzerland and Liechtenstein** is based in Zurich; it collects donations and informs people about children's rights. With its “Child-friendly Municipality” programme it gives awards to municipalities that involve children especially well. Well-known personalities support UNICEF as ambassadors. The actress Audrey Hepburn, who spent the last part of her life in Switzerland, was one of the most famous UNICEF ambassadors.

begriffe.wort: Convention on the Rights of the Child
begriffe.erklaerung: A UN treaty that sets out the rights of all children.
An organisation that supports people in need.
Protection against an infectious disease by means of a vaccine.
The body gets too little food or too few nutrients.

gewusst: UNICEF obtains vaccines for almost half of all the children in the world.
Audrey Hepburn is buried in Tolochenaz on Lake Geneva, where she spent the last years of her life.

teile.einleitung: The crime of aggression means planning or waging a war of aggression that clearly violates the UN Charter. It is one of the most serious crimes under international law. Only the leaders of a state can be held responsible.
wichtigste: The crime is defined in Art. 8 bis of the Rome Statute.
Art. 8 bis was added in 2010 at the conference in Kampala.
Since 17 July 2018 the International Criminal Court has been able to prosecute it.
Only someone who actually directs the leadership of a state can be a perpetrator.
Only a manifest violation of the UN Charter counts.
At Nuremberg it was called a “crime against peace”.
In 2012 Liechtenstein was the first state to ratify the amendments.

abschnitte.text: After the **Second World War**, leading figures of Nazi Germany were put on trial in **Nuremberg**. There, planning and waging a war of aggression was charged as a **crime against peace**. The judgment called the war of aggression the **“supreme international crime”**, because it contains within itself all the other evils. After that, however, it took decades for states to agree on an exact definition.

The **International Criminal Court** (ICC) in The Hague is based on the **Rome Statute**. At the **Review Conference** in **Kampala**, Uganda, in **2010**, **Art. 8 bis** was added. It defines the crime of aggression. For comparison: **Art. 6** concerns genocide and **Art. 7** crimes against humanity. At the end of 2017 the states parties decided to activate the court's jurisdiction. It has applied since **17 July 2018**.

Aggression is a **leadership crime**. Only someone who effectively controls the **political or military action** of a state can be a perpetrator. Ordinary soldiers therefore cannot be charged with aggression. In addition, not every border incident is enough. By its **character, gravity and scale**, the act of aggression must be a **manifest violation** of the UN Charter.

**Liechtenstein** strongly shaped the negotiations. Its UN ambassador **Christian Wenaweser** chaired the Assembly of States Parties. In **2012** Liechtenstein was the first state to ratify the **Kampala amendments**. The ICC cannot prosecute aggression by citizens of states that are not parties. That is why Ukraine and the **Council of Europe** agreed in Strasbourg in **June 2025** on a **special tribunal** for the aggression against Ukraine. It was signed by President Zelensky and Secretary General **Alain Berset**, a former Swiss federal councillor.

gewusst: As early as 1974 the UN General Assembly described in a resolution what counts as an act of aggression.
The court in Nuremberg was the first to convict individuals for a war of aggression.

teile.einleitung: UNESCO is the United Nations organisation for education, science and culture. It is best known for its World Heritage List, which includes famous buildings and natural wonders. There are many such World Heritage Sites in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: UNESCO works for education, science and culture.
It was founded in November 1945 and is based in Paris.
The abbreviation stands for “United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization”.
The World Heritage Convention to protect special places has existed since 1972.
Over 1200 sites worldwide are on the World Heritage List (as of 2025).
Switzerland has 13 World Heritage Sites, including the Old City of Bern and the Jungfrau-Aletsch area.
UNESCO also protects living traditions such as the Basel Carnival.

abschnitte.text: **UNESCO** is a specialised agency of the United Nations based in Paris. It was founded on 16 November 1945, shortly after the Second World War. The idea was: if people know more about each other and learn together, fewer wars will happen. Today almost all the states of the world are members, Switzerland since 1949.

One main aim is for every child to be able to go to school and learn to read and write. Many millions of children worldwide still do not go to school, especially girls in poor countries. UNESCO helps countries to build schools and train teachers. For example, it organises **International Literacy Day** on 8 September.

With the **World Heritage Convention** of 1972, states commit themselves to protecting especially valuable places. These include buildings such as the Pyramids of Giza or the Great Wall of China and natural wonders such as the Grand Canyon. If a World Heritage Site is threatened, it is put on the “red list” of World Heritage in Danger. Every year a committee decides which new places are added.

Switzerland's sites include the **Old City of Bern**, the Abbey of St Gall and the Benedictine Convent of St John at Müstair. The three castles of Bellinzona, the Lavaux vineyard terraces and the Rhaetian Railway on the Albula and Bernina lines are also World Heritage. Natural heritage sites are the Jungfrau-Aletsch region, Monte San Giorgio and the Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona. They also include, among others, the watchmaking towns of La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle.

Since 2003 UNESCO has also protected **intangible cultural heritage**, meaning traditions, festivals and crafts. From Switzerland these include the Basel Carnival, avalanche risk management and the craft of watchmaking, which was listed together with France. Such traditions only live on if people keep them up and pass them on. UNESCO also promotes science, for example ocean research.

begriffe.erklaerung: Places that are so valuable that they are protected for all of humanity.
An independent organisation that is closely linked to the UN.
Culture you cannot touch, such as customs, music or craft knowledge.
People learning to read and write.

gewusst: The Rhaetian Railway on the Albula and Bernina lines is one of the few railway lines in the world that are World Heritage.
At Monte San Giorgio in Ticino many fossils of marine reptiles from the Triassic period have been found.
